lessons.title_en: Staying safe while using a computer

body_json.title: Two sides of safety
bullets: Physical safety: protecting your eyes, neck, back and wrists from long hours at a computer.
Information safety: protecting your device, files and personal details from harmful programs and scammers.
Today we learn both, step by step.

scenes.captions: Computers and phones are big helpers for study and work. But using them carries two kinds of risk. One is to the body: long hours at a screen can hurt your eyes, neck and back. The other is to information: viruses or scammers can steal or damage your files and personal details. Today we learn how to stay safe from both.

bullets: The top of the monitor at or a little below eye level, about 50-70 cm from your eyes.
Back straight, feet flat on the floor, knees at about a right angle.
Keep your wrists straight while typing.

scenes.captions: The picture shows how to sit. The top edge of the monitor should be at eye level or a little lower, about an arm's length away. Back straight, both feet on the floor, knees at about ninety degrees. Keep your wrists straight when you type; do not bend them. The science of arranging equipment to fit the body like this is called ergonomics.

body_json.title: Breaks for your eyes and body
bullets: The 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds.
Once an hour, get up, walk and loosen your neck and shoulders.
Keep the room well lit and the screen brightness close to the room's light.

scenes.captions: Staring at a screen nonstop makes your eyes dry and tired. Remember one easy rule: twenty, twenty, twenty. Every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. And once an hour, get up and walk a little. A bright screen in a dark room is hard on the eyes, so keep the room lit.

question.stem: Under the 20-20-20 rule, what do you do every 20 minutes?
question.explanation: Looking at something far away relaxes the eye muscles. So: 20 feet away, for 20 seconds.

scenes.captions: Do you remember? What does the twenty-twenty-twenty rule ask you to do?

body_json.title: Malware: harmful programs
bullets: A program made on purpose to cause harm is called malware.
A virus spreads by attaching itself to other files. A worm spreads by itself across a network. A Trojan disguises itself as a useful program.
Signs: the computer suddenly slows down, files vanish or break, strange pop-ups appear.

scenes.captions: Now, information safety. Some programs are made only to do harm. Together we call them malware. A virus spreads by sticking to other files, for example from an infected pen drive. A worm moves from computer to computer over a network by itself. A Trojan arrives dressed up as a nice game or app. If your computer suddenly gets very slow or strange pop-ups appear, be suspicious.

body_json.title: How to stay safe from malware
bullets: Use antivirus software and keep it updated.
Download software only from trusted sources. Scan a pen drive before opening it.
Keep backups of important files on another drive or in the cloud.

scenes.captions: There are three ways to stay safe. One, keep antivirus software and update it often, because new viruses appear every day. Two, download software only from trusted places, and scan a friend's pen drive before you open it. Three, keep a copy of important files somewhere else. That is called a backup. Even if everything breaks, you can get your files back.

question.stem: Which malware arrives disguised as a useful program?
question.explanation: A Trojan looks like a good program but hides harmful code inside. Antivirus and firewalls are actually there to protect you.

scenes.captions: Tell me, which one comes disguised as a good program?

body_json.title: Strong passwords
bullets: At least 12 characters, mixing capital and small letters, numbers and symbols.
Nothing easy to guess like your name, birthday, phone number or "123456".
A different password for each account, shared with nobody. Turn on two-step verification (2FA) where you can.

scenes.captions: Your password is the lock on your account's door. A strong one has at least twelve characters, mixing capital and small letters, numbers and symbols. Do not use your name or birthday; they are easy to guess. Use a different password for each account, so if one leaks the others stay safe. And with two-step verification on, nobody can get in even if they learn your password.

body_json.title: Online scams and cyberbullying
bullets: Phishing: fake messages or links pretending to be a bank or a known organisation, asking for your password or OTP. Never give your OTP to anyone.
Cyberbullying: frightening, insulting or harassing someone online.
If it happens, do not reply. Keep screenshots, block and report, and tell a parent or teacher. National helpline: 999.

scenes.captions: One last idea. If someone pretends to be a bank or phone company and asks for your password or OTP, that is phishing, a scam. Real organisations never ask for your OTP. And if someone frightens or insults you online, that is cyberbullying. Do not reply; keep screenshots, block and report, and always tell an adult. You are not alone.

questions.stem: What is the general name for programs made to cause harm?
questions.explanation: Malicious + software = malware. Viruses, worms and Trojans are all malware.

questions.stem: Which spreads by itself across a network without the user's help?
questions.explanation: A worm does not need to attach to other files; it copies itself and spreads.

questions.stem: What is the science of fitting equipment and the workplace to the body called?
questions.explanation: Following ergonomics reduces neck, back and wrist pain.

questions.stem: Where should the top edge of the monitor be while working?

options: At or slightly below eye level

questions.explanation: At or a little below eye level, you do not need to bend your neck.
It is long and mixes capitals, small letters, a number and symbols. The others are easy to guess.

questions.stem: What is the best way to get files back even if a virus damages them?
questions.explanation: A copy kept on another drive or in the cloud lets you restore the files.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the 20-20-20 rule?
questions.explanation: Looking far away regularly lets the eye muscles rest.

questions.stem: Which is a likely sign of a computer virus?

options: The computer suddenly becomes very slow for no reason
The clock shows the right time

questions.explanation: Malware secretly uses the processor and memory, so the computer slows down.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of turning on two-step verification (2FA)?

options: Even with the password, nobody gets in without the second code

questions.explanation: The second code usually comes only to your phone, so a thief cannot get in with the password alone.

questions.stem:
To stay safe from malware:

i. keep antivirus software updated

ii. scan a pen drive before opening it

iii. download free games from unknown websites

Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Software from unknown sources often hides Trojans, so iii is wrong.

questions.stem:
Features of a strong password:

i. at least 12 characters

ii. the same password for every account

iii. a mix of letters, numbers and symbols

Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Using one password everywhere means one leak puts every account at risk, so ii is wrong.

questions.stem:
If someone harasses you online:

i. keep screenshots as evidence

ii. reply with insults of your own

iii. tell a parent or teacher

Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Replying makes things worse. Keep evidence, block and report, and tell an adult.

questions.stem: What kind of scam is Nabila facing?

options_json.context: Nabila gets a message: "Your mobile banking account will be closed. Go to this link now and enter your PIN and OTP." The bank's name in the link address is spelled slightly differently.

questions.explanation: Pretending to be a known organisation and using a fake link to ask for secret details is phishing.

questions.stem: What is the best thing for Nabila to do?

options: Quickly open the link and enter her PIN and OTP
Not open the link, and call the bank's official number to check
Enter only the PIN, not the OTP
options_json.context: Nabila gets a message: "Your mobile banking account will be closed. Go to this link now and enter your PIN and OTP." The bank's name in the link address is spelled slightly differently.

questions.explanation: Banks never ask for a PIN or OTP by message. Checking through the official number is safe.

questions.stem: Tanvir brought a pen drive from a friend and opened it on his computer without scanning it. A few days later the computer became very slow and some of his project files would not open. His sister Rima regularly keeps her files on Google Drive and keeps her antivirus updated.

marks_json.prompt: Explain the difference between a virus and a worm.
Explain the cause of the problem with Tanvir's computer and how to fix it.
Whose files are safer, Tanvir's or Rima's? Evaluate with reasons.

answer_json.model: A computer virus is a harmful program that attaches itself to other files or programs, copies itself to spread, and damages files or the system.

rubric.criterion: States it is a harmful program that spreads by attaching to other files

answer_json.model:
A virus needs to attach to another file and becomes active when the user runs that file.

A worm needs no host file; it spreads by itself, sending copies of itself across a network from one computer to another.

rubric.criterion: Virus depends on a host file
Worm spreads by itself over a network

answer_json.model:
Cause: the friend's pen drive probably carried a virus. Opening it without scanning let the virus in; it used up the processor and memory (so the computer slowed) and damaged files.

Fix: scan the whole computer with updated antivirus software to remove the virus, restore damaged files from a backup if one exists, and scan pen drives before opening them in future.

rubric.criterion: Identifies virus infection from the pen drive as the cause
Links it to the slowness and damaged files
Gives at least two correct fixes

answer_json.model:
Rima's files are safer.

First, Rima keeps her antivirus updated, so even new viruses are more likely to be caught. Tanvir opened a pen drive without scanning it.

Second, Rima has copies of her files on Google Drive (in the cloud). Even if her computer breaks or gets infected, she can get her files back. Tanvir has no backup, so his damaged files may be lost.

Still, the cloud account must be protected with a strong password and two-step verification, or it carries its own risk.

rubric.criterion: Clearly concludes Rima's files are safer
Role of updated antivirus
Role of the cloud backup
Considers a limit or extra precaution (password/2FA)

questions.stem: For online classes and games, Sadia uses a laptop about 6 hours a day. She lies in bed with the laptop on her stomach, and at night she turns off the room light and keeps the screen at full brightness. Lately her eyes burn and her neck hurts.

marks_json.prompt: Using the passage, explain why Sadia's eyes burn and her neck hurts.
Propose a workable plan to fix Sadia's health problems and analyse why it would work.

answer_json.model: Ergonomics is the science of designing and arranging equipment and the workplace to fit the human body.

rubric.criterion: Correct definition

answer_json.model:
After every 20 minutes of screen use, look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds.

Looking at a close screen nonstop keeps the eye muscles tight; looking far away relaxes them and reduces eye strain.

rubric.criterion: States the rule correctly
Explains why it relaxes the eyes

answer_json.model:
Neck pain: lying down with the laptop on her stomach puts the screen far below eye level, so she keeps her neck bent forward for a long time. This strains the neck muscles.

Burning eyes: a full-brightness screen in a dark room strains the eyes. On top of that, 6 hours a day without breaks means she blinks less and her eyes dry out.

rubric.criterion: Links neck pain to poor posture and screen position
Links eye pain to a bright screen in the dark
Mentions the effect of long use without breaks

answer_json.model:
1. Work at a table and chair: back straight, feet on the floor. Raise the laptop on books or a stand so the top of the screen is at eye level, with a separate keyboard if needed. Then she will not bend her neck.

2. Keep the room light on and set screen brightness close to the room's light; use night mode at night. This reduces eye strain.

3. Follow the 20-20-20 rule and get up to walk every hour.

4. Limit game time to cut total screen time.

The plan works because it tackles the root cause of each problem (posture, lighting, nonstop use) directly, and needs no expensive equipment.

rubric.criterion: Proposes fixing posture and screen height
Proposes fixing lighting and brightness
Proposes breaks or less screen time
Justifies each step by linking it to a cause

method_sheets.body_md:
# Situation-based creative questions (computer safety)

## Spot it
- The passage shows someone with a problem: a slow computer, damaged files, sore eyes or neck, a suspicious message.
- Often two people are compared: one careful, one careless.

## Steps
1. (a) Knowledge: a one-sentence definition. Keep the key words (for example "harmful program", "attaches to other files").
2. (b) Comprehension: two sentences on the idea, then why or how.
3. (c) Application: point to the cause in the passage, name the idea from the lesson, then link it to the result. Start with "The passage shows...".
4. (d) Higher-order: a clear conclusion first (who is safer / what should be done), then 2-3 reasons, and finally one limit or extra precaution.

## Common trap
- Writing memorised text without using details from the passage.
- In (d), describing without giving a conclusion.
- Mixing up viruses, worms and Trojans.

## Lesson link
Every idea is in the lesson "Staying safe while using a computer".
